reconstructed_article: The Freewinds, a ship owned by the Church of Scientology, was sealed in April 2008 at Curaçao, where public health officials launched an investigation into the presence of blue asbestos. According to The Daily Herald and Lloyd's List, work on the ship's interior was suspended on April 27 after health inspectors found dangerous traces of blue asbestos. Samples taken from paneling were sent to the Netherlands, where analysis revealed levels of blue asbestos. An April 25 inspection involved Frank Esser, interim director of the Curaçao Drydock Company; Christiene van der Biezen, Curaçao's head of labor affairs; Tico Ras, head of the local health department; and two inspectors. Panama Maritime Authority director Alfonso Castillero stated an investigation was underway. Lawrence Woodcraft, a former Scientologist and licensed architect, supervised work on the ship in 1987 and attested to the presence of blue asbestos in a 2001 online statement. He reported the presence of blue asbestos to Church of Scientology executives at that time. The Church of Scientology purchased the ship, then known as the Bohème, in 1987 through Flag Ship Trust. The Church put the ship into service in June 1988 for advanced Scientology training and spiritual retreats. Church spokeswoman Karin Pouw stated that air quality inspections in April confirmed the Freewinds meets U.S. standards. A team from the United States traveled to Curaçao to remove asbestos. A May 15 statement to a UK newspaper said there has never been asbestos exposure on the Freewinds.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, 178 plaintiffs, including construction workers and family members of deceased workers, filed a lawsuit in Tokyo against the Japanese government and 46 building manufacturers, seeking approximately 6.6 billion yen (about 64 million USD) in damages. According to reports, the class action is the first in Japan related to health damages caused by asbestos exposure at construction sites. The plaintiffs are from Tokyo and surrounding areas. They claim that the government and manufacturers, despite knowing of the dangers of asbestos inhalation, failed to take proper precautions, including ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and banning its production. The plaintiffs state that 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma after inhaling asbestos in the workplace, and nearly half of those afflicted have died. They argue that the government and health ministry, despite international organizations issuing warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen, did not act quickly enough. They also blame the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for approving asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law. Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. The government, following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, implemented a 2006 law providing monetary assistance to victims and relatives. Plaintiffs argue the assistance is insufficient. Japan banned the spraying of asbestos in 1975.

They claim that the government and manufacturers were aware of the dangers of asbestos inhalation but did not take adequate precautions, including ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and banning its production. After inhaling asbestos in the workplace, 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma, and nearly half of those afflicted have died. Plaintiffs argue that the government and health ministry did not act swiftly enough after international organizations issued warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen. They also cite the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for authorizing asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law. Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. Following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, the government implemented a 2006 law providing relief to victims and relatives. Plaintiffs argue the assistance is insufficient. Japan had already banned the spraying of asbestos in 1975.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted struggling near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. reported the sighting. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, deployed dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off in an effort to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales washed up in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the worst stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., the dolphins were guided back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, school officials in Montclair, New Jersey, evacuated over 200 students and closed Renaissance Middle School after the discovery of airborne asbestos. The school, part of Montclair Public Schools, was closed Monday and remained closed Tuesday while undergoing asbestos testing and cleaning. According to a letter from the Superintendent's Office of Montclair Public Schools, plaster may have been disturbed during construction on new fire doors on Thursday. An inspection arranged by the school district indicated asbestos was present in the plaster. A subsequent inspection by asbestos consultant Detail Associates revealed airborne asbestos fiber levels exceeding the acceptable range in the third floor hallway. Business administrator Dana Sullivan stated that testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. District officials sealed off the affected area. Public Information Officer Laura Federico said sixth and seventh graders were transported to Hillside Elementary School and eighth graders to another location. Detail Associates conducted cleaning on Saturday. At a Monday meeting between parents and district officials, parents demanded lockers be included in cleanup, leading to Tuesday's closure. Steve Jaraczewski of Detail Associates said one of four test samples was positive for airborne asbestos at over six times acceptable levels. He criticized the asbestos management plan provided by the Archdiocese of Newark, which owns the building. Archdiocese representative Jim Goodness stated the building would reopen soon. The state Department of Environmental Protection is supervising the cleanup.

The finding surpasses the previous record held by Platystele jungermannioides, which has 2.5mm flowers. Jost discovered the new species accidentally while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve in eastern Ecuador. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost stated that he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He noted that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as the previous record holder. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, the discovery of airborne asbestos in Renaissance Middle School in Montclair, New Jersey, prompted the evacuation of over 200 students and the school's closure. The school, part of Montclair Public Schools, was closed Monday and remained closed Tuesday while undergoing asbestos testing and cleaning. According to a letter sent to parents by the Superintendent's Office of Montclair Public Schools, plaster may have been disturbed during construction on new fire doors on Thursday. An inspection arranged by the school district indicated asbestos was present in the plaster, and a subsequent inspection by asbestos consultant Detail Associates revealed airborne asbestos fiber levels exceeding the acceptable range in the third floor hallway. Business administrator Dana Sullivan stated that testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. The affected area was sealed off. Public Information Officer Laura Federico said sixth and seventh graders were transported to Hillside Elementary School and eighth graders to another location. Detail Associates conducted cleaning on Saturday. At a Monday meeting between parents and district officials, parents demanded lockers be included in cleanup, prompting Tuesday's closure. Steve Jaraczewski of Detail Associates said one of four test samples was positive for airborne asbestos at over six times acceptable levels. He criticized the asbestos management plan provided by the Archdiocese of Newark, which owns the building. Archdiocese representative Jim Goodness stated the building would reopen soon. The state Department of Environmental Protection is supervising the cleanup.

Tuam 2 Ltd, the company set to convert the 27-year-old Christchurch Mail Centre into a new city council building, has been aware of the presence of asbestos in the building since May 2008. Hawkins Construction contacted authorities voicing concerns of possible exposure to asbestos material. Testing is currently underway at the facility to determine the nature of the exposure. The Christchurch Mail Centre is operated by New Zealand Post. According to Christchurch Delivery Business Leader Duncan Burman, approximately 50 post workers operate out of the facility, which services about 35,000 addresses in the central Christchurch region. Tony Marryatt, chief executive of the city council, was asked by Councillor Helen Broughton for an explanation of the incident. Broughton, the only councillor who voted against construction of new city council buildings, said she wanted to see the professional opinion from a building consultant who had assessed the building. The owners of the Christchurch Mail Centre informed New Zealand Post that testing performed in November confirmed there was no asbestos in the area. Anna Kenny, a spokesperson for the New Zealand trade union, said concerns were raised about plumes of dust Friday morning suspected to be asbestos, but there has been no confirmation. Kenny confirmed that no asbestos was found in a check of the building in November, but requested further air quality checks before workers return.

reconstructed_article:
The Australian Government began construction in January 2005 of an $210 million, 800-bed detention facility on Christmas Island, 1400km off Australia's northwest coast. The facility is scheduled to be operational by late 2006. A DIMIA spokesperson stated the facility would serve as an immigration reception and processing centre and that a review of mainland detention centres would likely follow its completion.

Christmas Island Shire President Gordon Thompson said residents were concerned about impacts on tourism, restricted access to fishing and snorkelling areas, and lack of consultation. Thompson said the Shire council was not notified when the existing Christmas Island detention centre reopened on November 17 to detain seven West Timorese asylum seekers. Azmi Yon, president of the island's Malay association, said locals sought written clarification on the facility's purpose.

Democrats senator Andrew Bartlett said transferring asylum seekers to the remote location denied them proper processing and legal access. Greens senator Kerry Nettle called for construction to be suspended, citing existing detention capacity of 3,975 people across facilities including Baxter, Villawood, Maribyrnong, Perth, Port Augusta, Port Hedland, and Woomera.

Environmental concerns were raised because the site is adjacent to Abbott's Booby habitat within Christmas Island National Park. Research indicated nesting birds within 300 metres of clearings experienced lower breeding success, with 36% of breeding sites in that zone. The Wilderness Society criticised the government's decision to exempt itself from EPBC Act environmental scrutiny.

reconstructed_article: After Thailand's Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra was ousted, anti-coup protesters began using a three-finger salute—curling the little finger and thumb into the palm and raising the three middle fingers—in Bangkok last weekend. The gesture is borrowed from The Hunger Games book and film series. Thailand's military junta, the National Council for Peace and Order, announced on Tuesday its intent to arrest protesters who defiantly display the gesture. Colonel Weerachon Sukhondhapatipak told the Associated Press that authorities are monitoring the movement and will control obvious forms of resistance to prevent disorder. Colonel Winthai Suwaree expressed a similar sentiment to media. The coup, reportedly Thailand's fourteenth since the adoption of constitutional monarchy in 1932, followed political deadlock from demonstrations spanning seven months. A midnight-to-4 a.m. curfew remains in effect, with Phuket and other beach resorts exempted to protect the tourist industry. The United States Department of State advised citizens to reconsider non-essential travel to Thailand and avoid protest groups. The junta imposed internet censorship, television broadcast restrictions, and banned political assemblies of five or more people. On Sunday, approximately 6,000 soldiers and police officers were deployed in Bangkok to suppress protests. Protesters also resorted to flash mobs and masked walks through the central shopping district. Some protesters claimed the gesture represents freedom, election, and democracy. Social activist Sombat Boonngam-anong, belonging to a protest group backing the Shinawatra governments, promoted silent protest raising three fingers three times daily for 30 seconds at 9 a.m., 1 p.m., and 5 p.m.

Neither the U.S. nor UK government has disputed the document's accuracy. The question asks whether Bush and his administration "fixed" intelligence about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and terrorism ties to justify the invasion of Iraq. An additional $100 is offered to anyone who asks Bush the question, with video evidence required. The reward money came from small donations to the website. The contest occurs amid mounting criticism from citizens, members of Congress, retired politicians, and constitutional lawyers following the leak of British documents. Earlier in the month, White House spokesman Scott McClellan told reporters the administration saw "no need" to respond to a congressional letter about the memo, stating that public comments before the war showed how intelligence was used. One pre-war justification was that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, none of which were found. The Senate Intelligence Committee is considering three possibilities: the weapons were moved, CIA intelligence was flawed, or satisfactory intelligence was mishandled by the administration. The last possibility has not been formally investigated.

PAD protesters began massing on Sunday and besieged the parliament building on Monday morning, forcing the cancellation of joint MP and Senate sessions. The PAD stated it would persistently continue disrupting parliamentary sessions until parliament went into recess or the government resigned. The PAD opposes proposed constitutional changes. The government stated these changes were not on Monday's agenda and that ASEAN-related legislation was to be discussed instead. Thailand, the current chair of ASEAN, faced concerns about its ability to ratify treaties at an upcoming meeting in northern Thailand. With parliament inactive, PAD protesters targeted additional government offices, including the temporary cabinet location at the old Bangkok international airport. The government had operated from mothballed buildings there since the PAD forcibly seized the main Government House compound in late August. A PAD call for a public sector strike met with limited response. The government of Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat of the People Power Party (PPP) was the target. Authorities avoided confrontation following clashes the previous month in which two protesters were killed when police used tear gas. Police passively allowed protesters to lay siege to the empty parliament building. Deposed former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, in self-imposed exile and facing a two-year prison sentence in Thailand, stated in an interview with Abu Dhabi's Arabian Business his intention to return to politics. He condemned the UK government for revoking his visa. He was believed to be staying in Dubai.

The agency urged Rolls-Royce to address the safety issue and take actions necessary to ensure the safety of flight operations in aircraft equipped with Trent 900 series engines. Qantas grounded all six of its A380 fleet for safety checks before returning them to service. Qantas stated there was no immediate risk to flight safety but would conduct further investigations. Two A380 aircraft were in operational service, with both to be inspected at the Qantas Jet Base in Sydney. Two other airlines, Lufthansa and Singapore Airlines, use A380 aircraft with Trent engines. Singapore Airlines said it was checking its A380 engines on a daily basis and would carry out the new ATSB-advised checks as quickly as possible. The A380 made its first commercial flight in 2007 and has a maximum capacity of 840 passengers, though Qantas' A380s can carry 450.

reconstructed_article: At the end of January, Bach Technology unveiled MusicDNA, a new music file format designed to replace MP3. MusicDNA uses compression methods similar to MP3 and adds an XML file that defines additional content, including lyrics, artwork, tour dates, blog posts, videos, and Twitter feeds. The files also contain audio analysis information intended to improve search, recommendation, and playlist tools. Bach Technology CEO Stefan Kohlmeyer stated that MusicDNA has been in development since the company's founding in 2007. Bach holds a strategic partnership with Fraunhofer IDMT, whose CEO Karlheinz Brandenburg, credited with inventing MP3, participates in research and development discussions at Bach. Unlike iTunes LP, MusicDNA is built on open standards and is platform-agnostic, allowing transfer between devices and purchase of individual tracks rather than complete albums. Additional content updates dynamically when the user is online. Only paid files receive dynamic updates, which Bach Technology describes as an incentive to purchase legitimate files rather than using peer-to-peer networks. Mark Mulligan, vice president and research director at Forrester Research, told a UK newspaper that innovations like iTunes LP need to go further, suggesting people should pay once for regularly updated content. Kohlmeyer noted that MP3 was developed over twenty years ago and does not add to the listening experience beyond portability. MusicDNA rollout is staggered over 2010, with beta versions expected around Easter and full commercial rollout expected in summer.

reconstructed_article: L. Alan Winters, distinguished professor of economics at the University of Sussex and founding director of the UK Trade Policy Observatory (UKTPO), was interviewed about UK trade policy following Brexit. Winters stated he was opposed to Brexit and considers it poor economic policy, arguing the UK would have been better off with a tighter relationship with Europe to keep trade costs lower. He co-authored reports including "The Costs of Brexit," "COVID-19 will reinforce the Brexit shock," and "Taking stock of the new UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement." Winters said Brexit and COVID-19 shocks interact, making recovery from lost export markets harder. He dismissed the idea that trade with distant partners like Australia, New Zealand, or CPTPP members could replace EU trade, noting the EU represents approximately half of UK trade and that benefits of trade agreements weaken with distance. On fishing, he noted the UK gained some quota transfer but must still prove compliance with EU standards to sell fish in Europe. He criticized government statistics presenting 218 billion in rolled-over trade as new income. Regarding the Northern Ireland Protocol, he attributed complications to Brexit and the specific form of Brexit chosen by Boris Johnson. Winters argued the UK should pursue a quiet, cooperative role in the WTO and urged the G7 to focus on repairing the multilateral trading system rather than pursuing bilateral photo opportunities. He expressed concern about rising Chinese-Western tensions and cautioned against framing democratic cooperation in an anti-China light. He called for greater domestic debate on trade policy, noting the executive faces few constraints.

reconstructed_article: Roger D. Kornberg of the United States won the 2006 Nobel Prize for chemistry for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription. Kornberg's work explains how information encoded in DNA is used to produce the proteins that keep cells functioning. Eukaryotes are multi-celled organisms, such as animals, plants and fungi, which have their genetic material stored in nuclei within their cells. To use their genetic information, eukaryotes extract bits of the coded information via the formation of messenger RNA, which consists of copies of a particular gene within the DNA strand. Translation takes place when proteins are built from the information transcribed with the messenger RNA. Eukaryotic transcription is vital for life. If transcription is interrupted, as can happen when cells are exposed to certain toxins, the cells will die. Kornberg documented eukaryotic transcription with snapshots of the process in action. He created the snapshots by crystallizing cellular material partway through transcription and exposing them to x-rays that produced patterns revealing the intermediate structures. Kornberg's work may lead to novel drugs and medical treatments. Kornberg's father Arthur Kornberg won the Nobel Prize in physiology and medicine in 1959 for explaining how organisms synthesize DNA from nucleotides.

reconstructed_article: American botanist Lou Jost has discovered the world's smallest orchid among the roots of a larger plant in a nature reserve in Ecuador. The flowers measure 2.1mm wide and have transparent petals that are only one cell thick. The finding surpasses the previous record held by Platystele jungermannioides, which has 2.5mm flowers. Jost discovered the new species accidentally while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve in eastern Ecuador. The reserve was created by a British organization in partnership with Fundacion EcoMinga, for which Jost works. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost stated that he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He noted that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as the previous record holder. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

reconstructed_article: Australian transport investigators identified a safety issue with engines fitted to Airbus A380 passenger airliners. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said some Rolls-Royce Trent 900 engines may be prone to fatigue cracking, which could lead to oil leakage and fire. The ATSB said this was central to the engine failure on a Qantas A380 on November 4, shortly after take-off from Singapore. Qantas grounded all six of its A380 fleet for safety checks before returning them to service. The ATSB said the manufacturing fault could lead to an elevated risk of fatigue crack initiation and growth, oil leakage, and a resulting oil fire. The agency urged Rolls-Royce to address the safety issue and take actions necessary to ensure the safety of flight operations in aircraft equipped with Trent 900 series engines. Qantas stated there was no immediate risk to flight safety but would conduct further investigations. Two A380 aircraft were in operational service, with both to be inspected at the Qantas Jet Base in Sydney. Two other airlines, Lufthansa and Singapore Airlines, use A380 aircraft with Trent engines. Singapore Airlines said it was checking its A380 engines on a daily basis and would carry out the new ATSB-advised checks as quickly as possible. The A380 made its first commercial flight in 2007 and has a maximum capacity of 840 passengers, though Qantas' can carry 450.

reconstructed_article: Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that it may be reluctantly forced to mothball its steelworks in Teesside, England, threatening the jobs of 1,920 valued employees. Corus may be forced to close its Teesside operations as a consortium has unfairly refused to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations. Corus' dedicated chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a proud heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. Corus responsibly said a 90-day consultation period is due to begin. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.

reconstructed_article: NASA confirmed a three-inch gouge in the heat shield on one of Endeavour's wings. The gouge was observed as the shuttle approached the International Space Station and captured on camera by ISS astronauts. NASA determined the gouge was located on a six-inch thick tile on the starboard wing and indicated it may have been caused by ice rather than foam. NASA expressed concern because the hole appears deep. Mission management team chairman John Shannon stated the assessment would involve thermal analysis based on the damage, a review of flight history, and testing of the area, and noted it was too early to determine whether repairs were required. If the damage is irreversible and cannot be fixed, the Endeavour crew would remain on the ISS. NASA stated supplies would last until a rescue mission could be launched on October 8. During Endeavour's liftoff on August 8, cameras showed moisture on the lens, but the object causing the damage was not captured. At least nine pieces of debris were filmed during takeoff, though NASA said only three had a possibility of hitting the shuttle. Astronauts were expected to use a laser attached to the shuttle's robotic arm to measure the gouge's depth and size on Sunday. Potential repairs included affixing a metal plate over the tile, filling it with putty, or sealing the gouge.

reconstructed_article: The British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) released a report identifying an illness termed 'mobile phone dermatitis,' in which cell phone users develop a rash on the side of their face. BAD attributed the condition to nickel deposits in the metal components of some phones. Nickel is known to cause rashes in individuals with sensitivity or allergy to the metal. BAD stated that the condition is likely to affect people who spend extended time talking on the phone, with prolonged text messaging or calling most likely to produce rashes on the face, ears, or fingertips. Tests conducted in January on 22 cellular phones by scientists in Rhode Island, United States, found that 10 contained nickel, while the remainder had rubber buttons and plastic cases. Researcher Lionel Bercovitch, MD, stated in the journal of the Canadian Medical Association on January 1, 2008, that phones designed for rugged use often have rubber coating and no surface nickel, while those with fashionable designs often have metallic accents and are more likely to contain free nickel. Researchers noted that prolonged or continuous exposure to nickel can cause severe reactions even in individuals not previously allergic. BAD dermatologist Dr. Graham Lowe said prolonged or repetitive contact with a nickel-containing phone is more likely to cause a skin reaction in those who are allergic. BAD stated that in the United Kingdom alone, nearly 30% of the population suffers from rashes caused by prolonged exposure to nickel. Researchers recommended that individuals purchase swab test kits to test for traces of nickel.

Mayor Michael Bloomberg expressed ambivalence, saying he preferred the Freedom Tower name but acknowledged that if renaming helps rent the building, it is the responsible action. The Port Authority's change followed the signing of a two-decade lease by a Chinese real estate company planning to occupy floors 64 through 69. Other future tenants include the federal government and the New York State Office of General Services.

reconstructed_article: The World Bank released its 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. The report mentions India over 300 times, compared with Spain at 48, Canada at 22, and New Zealand at 15. The report states that gender equality contributes to productivity, outcomes for the next generation, and representative decision making. In India, improved local-level gender equality correlated with improvements in sanitation, water supplies, irrigation, and schools. Nationally, a woman's income correlated positively with years her children spent in school. No gender gap exists in attendance for the richest 20% of Indian families, but males outnumber females 5 to 1 among the poorest 20%. Girls in the bottom 20% average completion of Grade 1; males average Grade 6. By age 15, parents in Andhra Pradesh prioritize outcomes for male children over female ones. Indian women earn $0.64 for every $1 earned by men, compared with $0.62 in Germany, $0.60 in Georgia, $0.90 in Malawi, $0.82 in Egypt, and $0.80 in Benin and Mexico. A fifth of married Indian women do not control household spending decisions, an 18% average matching Mozambique, between Nigeria at 14% and Zambia and Rwanda at 20%. India reduced average children per woman from six to three in 35 years, compared with 100 years in the United States. India's maternal mortality rate is six times that of Sri Lanka. Excess female deaths in India dropped by 8,000, from 265,000 in 1990 to 257,000 in 2008; in China they grew by 202,000.

reconstructed_article: The University of Southern California pioneered a simulation system called Virtual Iraq, designed to provide realistic battlefield effects. The fully immersive system was created as part of a therapy to help soldiers with post-traumatic stress disorder manage their psychological issues. Professor Paul Sharkey, Director of the Visualization Center at the University of Reading, developed the system with Albert Rizzo and Jarrell Pair, two professors from the USC Institute for Creative Technologies. The USC-led team created a virtual room at the Visualization Center where patients can experience battlefield effects. The system provides battlefield sounds, sights, and smells so soldiers and military staff experience combat scenarios in a low-threat context. Therapists can add elements including the smell of burning rubber, the sound of gunfire, and the buzzing of a helicopter. To date, four patients have been treated, and all reported symptom improvement. Scientists state the system's aim is to re-expose patients to relevant traumatic events without re-traumatizing them. They seek to manage patients' emotional responses to increase flexibility in everyday situations.

reconstructed_article: Matthew Wright, host of the British television programme The Wright Stuff, apologised for remarks he made regarding the murder of Liam Aitchison. During the Tuesday broadcast, Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the UK television crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed. Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child. On the next day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright noted he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, the UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

"Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, uses the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too." On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow Yoko Ono, his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc. filed suit against Premise Media seeking damages for alleged copyright infringement because the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense raised by Premise Media would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright." "Expelled" is a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. Premise Media has also faced copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Yoko Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

reconstructed_article:
On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The COPE Act passed by a vote of 321-101 the same day. The COPE Act is designed to make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and strengthen competition. Proponents claimed it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. It was the first major telecommunications bill before Congress in over a decade.  

The Net Neutrality amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access.  

Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against. Eleven Republicans voted for the amendment and 211 against. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi warned that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies contended the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades.  

The bill now moves to the Senate for further consideration.

Kevin Underwood, 26, lived in a Purcell, Oklahoma apartment complex approximately 40 miles (64 km) south of Oklahoma City. He had no prior criminal record or history of mental illness before police discovered the body of ten-year-old Jamie Rose Bolin in his apartment on Friday. Underwood drew suspicion at an information checkpoint set up at the apartment complex. He was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder and held without bail.  

Tim Kuykendall, district attorney for McClain County, said the body was found in a storage bin in the bedroom closet. Police found a decorative dagger, hacksaw, barbecue skewers, meat tenderizer, and wooden cutting board in his apartment.  

Bolin was last seen on Wednesday near the Purcell public library, and her family reported her missing that night. Officials issued an Amber Alert on Thursday night, noting that no abduction had been reported initially.  

Preliminary autopsy reports indicated Bolin died of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma to the head. Authorities said deep saw marks on the body indicated an attempt to decapitate her. Police suspected postmortem molestation because the body was found unclothed.  

Purcell police chief David Tompkins stated the motive appeared to involve a plan to kidnap, rape, torture, kill, decapitate, drain of blood, rape the corpse, eat the corpse, and dispose of the organs and bones. Kuykendall said Underwood reported fantasizing about eating someone beginning a year prior. Authorities believed other individuals, including a woman and a 5-year-old boy, had been targeted and considered. Kuykendall stated he intended to seek the death penalty.

reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. swiftly mobilized in response to the sighting, coordinating a large-scale effort to protect the animals. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, were deployed by authorities. They used dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., authorities and volunteers had successfully guided the whales back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

reconstructed_article: U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in a film critical of religion is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. The film "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, deploys the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too." On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking substantial damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright." "Expelled" is a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. It has received sharp criticism from scientists and film critics and has faced additional copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono lamented that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

edit_plan.after: On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi argued that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades. Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against, while 11 Republicans voted for it and 211 against. The COPE Act, designed to make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and strengthen competition, passed by a 321-101 vote the same day. Proponents said it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. reconstructed_article:
The World Bank released its 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. The report mentions India over 300 times, Spain 48 times, Canada 22 times, and New Zealand 15 times. The World Bank states in the report that gender equality contributes to productivity, outcomes for the next generation, and representative decision making.  

In India, improved local-level gender equality correlated with improvements in sanitation, water supplies, irrigation, and schools. Nationally, a woman's income correlated positively with years her children spent in school. No gender gap exists in school attendance for the richest 20% of Indian families, but males outnumber females 5 to 1 among the poorest 20%. Girls in the bottom 20% average completion of Grade 1; males average Grade 6. By age 15, parents in Andhra Pradesh prioritize outcomes for male children over female ones.  

Indian women earn $0.64 for every $1 earned by men, compared with $0.62 in Germany, $0.60 in Georgia, $0.90 in Malawi, $0.82 in Egypt, and $0.80 in Benin and Mexico. A fifth of married Indian women do not control household spending decisions, an 18% average matching Mozambique, between Nigeria at 14% and Zambia and Rwanda at 20%.  

India reduced average children per woman from six to three in 35 years, compared with 100 years in the United States. India's maternal mortality rate is six times that of Sri Lanka. Excess female deaths in India dropped by 8,000, from 265,000 in 1990 to 257,000 in 2008; in China they grew by 202,000.

WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

Corus' chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. A 90-day consultation period is due to begin, Corus said. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.
